subject: phy
title: Measurements and Uncertainties
subtitle: SI units, errors, uncertainties and significant figures.
concept: All physical measurements have uncertainties; distinguishing random from systematic errors is essential.
Absolute uncertainty gives the size of the error in the same units as the measurement; percentage uncertainty allows comparison.
Results should be quoted to an appropriate number of significant figures consistent with the uncertainty.

notes.heading: SI Units
items: The seven SI base units are: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and candela (cd). All other units are derived from these — e.g. newton (N = kg m s⁻²), pascal (Pa = N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²), joule (J = kg m² s⁻²).
Useful prefixes: nano (n, 10⁻⁹), micro (μ, 10⁻⁶), milli (m, 10⁻³), kilo (k, 10³), mega (M, 10⁶), giga (G, 10⁹). Always check unit consistency before substituting into formulae.

notes.heading: Errors
items: Random errors produce scatter about the true value — they are unpredictable and affect precision. Reduced by averaging many readings. Sources: reading a scale, timing reactions, vibrations.

Systematic errors shift every measurement in the same direction by the same amount — they affect accuracy, not precision. They cannot be reduced by averaging. Examples: a wrongly calibrated instrument, a non-zero reading before measurement (zero error), parallax error when reading a scale from an angle.
Precision: how reproducible the readings are (small spread). Accuracy: how close the mean value is to the true value. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (consistent systematic error).

notes.heading: Calculating and Combining Uncertainties
items: Absolute uncertainty (Δx): quoted in the same units as the measurement. For repeated readings: Δx = ½ × range. For a single reading from a digital instrument: Δx = ±1 in the last displayed digit; from an analogue scale: Δx = ±½ the smallest scale division.

When adding or subtracting quantities: add the absolute uncertainties. When multiplying or dividing: add the percentage uncertainties. When raising to a power n: multiply the percentage uncertainty by n.
Uncertainty in a gradient (from a graph): draw lines of maximum and minimum gradient consistent with the data; uncertainty = (max gradient − min gradient) / 2.

definitions.body: An unpredictable variation in repeated measurements; reduces precision but can be minimised by averaging multiple readings.
A consistent error in one direction affecting all measurements; reduces accuracy; cannot be reduced by averaging.
(Absolute uncertainty / measured value) × 100%; used when combining uncertainties in multiplied/divided quantities.

workedExamples.q: A ball's diameter is measured five times: 24.1, 24.3, 24.0, 24.2, 24.1 mm. Find the mean and uncertainty.
v = 12.0 ± 0.3 m s⁻¹; m = 2.50 ± 0.05 kg. Find KE = ½mv² with uncertainty.

mistakes: Multiplying percentage uncertainty by 2 when squaring — this IS correct (power rule); forgetting to do so is the error.
Giving uncertainty to too many significant figures — uncertainty should be 1–2 s.f. maximum.
Confusing random error (affects precision) with systematic error (affects accuracy).
tips: Resolution of an instrument ≠ its uncertainty; digital meters: uncertainty = ±1 in last digit; analogue: ±half the smallest division.
For a graph: uncertainty in gradient = (max gradient − min gradient) / 2.
Accuracy: how close to true value (systematic). Precision: how reproducible (random).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
flashcards.a: Accuracy: how close results are to the true value (affected by systematic errors). Precision: how reproducible/consistent results are (affected by random errors).

flashcards.q: How do you combine uncertainties when multiplying two quantities?
flashcards.a: Add the percentage uncertainties of each quantity.

flashcards.q: What is a systematic error? Give an example.
flashcards.a: A consistent error in one direction: e.g. a balance that reads 0.5 g too high (zero error); not reduced by averaging.

flashcards.q: State the seven SI base units.
flashcards.a: Metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

flashcards.q: A length L = 5.0 ± 0.2 m. What is the uncertainty in L²?
flashcards.a: % uncertainty in L = 4%; % uncertainty in L² = 2 × 4% = 8%; ΔL² = 0.08 × 25 = ±2.0 m².

questions.q: Which type of error cannot be reduced by repeating measurements and averaging?
questions.exp: Systematic errors shift all readings consistently; averaging repeated readings does not remove the offset.

questions.q: A = x × y². If %Δx = 3% and %Δy = 4%, what is %ΔA?
Five readings of resistance: 45, 47, 46, 48, 44 Ω. What is the uncertainty?
What does a small percentage uncertainty tell you?
opts: The measurement is precise (small random error relative to value)
questions.exp: Small percentage uncertainty means the absolute uncertainty is small relative to the measured value — the measurement is precise.

questions.q: Which is a derived SI unit?
questions.exp: Pascal (Pa) = N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² — derived from base units. The others are base units.
